skill_drafts.name: DTA Timestamp Conflict Detection
skill_drafts.description: Detect and resolve transaction conflicts by comparing transaction timestamps when two transactions access the same data. Use when implementing optimistic concurrency control with timestamp-based conflict detection to determine transaction ordering and identify conflicts.
skill_drafts.objective: Identify conflicting transactions via timestamp comparison and establish ordering
applicable_signals: Concurrent transaction access to shared data
OCC protocol active with timestamp-based conflict detection
Need to determine transaction serialization order
contraindications: Tuple-level timestamps are already maintained (use tuple-level conflict detection instead)
Pessimistic locking (2PL) is the primary concurrency strategy
Deadlock prevention via dependency graphs is the sole goal (use DTA deadlock detection instead)
workflow_steps: Retrieve timestamp associated with first transaction
Retrieve timestamp associated with second transaction
Return conflict determination and transaction ordering decision
triggers: Two transactions attempt to access overlapping data
Timestamp-based conflict resolution is required in OCC implementation
Transaction dependency must be established via timestamp ordering
constraints: Timestamps must be associated with transactions, not tuples
Comparison must occur at the point of data access conflict
Transaction timestamps must be comparable and ordered
cautions: DTA timestamp comparison has critical section bottleneck; does not scale beyond 16–32 active threads due to shared global resources
OCC with DTA timestamps requires considerable logic in critical section, limiting performance scalability
output_contract: Boolean conflict determination (true if conflict exists, false otherwise) and transaction ordering decision (which transaction should proceed first based on timestamp comparison)

metadata.prompt: When two transactions attempt to access overlapping data, compare their associated timestamps to determine conflict status and establish transaction ordering. In DTA, timestamps are transaction-level (not tuple-level) and are compared at conflict points to resolve dependencies.

skill_drafts.name: Critical Section Bottleneck Scaling Assessment
skill_drafts.description: Evaluate whether shared global resources in the critical section limit multi-threaded scalability. Identify and measure the point at which throughput plateaus due to centralized synchronization contention.
skill_drafts.objective: Identify and measure critical section contention impact on throughput
applicable_signals: Observed throughput plateau in scaling curve
Lock contention metrics indicate high critical section occupancy
Performance degradation correlates with thread count increase
contraindications: Lock-free or fully distributed algorithms are in use
Single-threaded performance is the primary focus
No shared global resources exist in the algorithm
workflow_steps: {'step': 1, 'action': 'Configure test harness with variable thread count parameter'}
{'step': 3, 'action': 'Measure and record throughput (transactions/sec or operations/sec) for each thread count'}
{'step': 5, 'action': 'Identify the thread count threshold where throughput plateaus or begins to degrade'}
{'step': 6, 'action': 'Collect lock contention or critical section profiling data at the identified threshold'}
{'step': 7, 'action': 'Confirm that critical section occupancy or lock wait time is the primary performance limiter'}
triggers: Throughput plateaus or degrades beyond 16–32 active threads
Shared global state is suspected as the cause of performance degradation
constraints: Test must use consistent workload across all thread counts
Thread count range should span from 1 to at least 2× the suspected scaling limit
Profiling or lock contention instrumentation must be available
cautions: Scaling behavior may vary with workload contention level; use representative workload
System thermal throttling or CPU frequency scaling may mask true contention effects
Ensure sufficient warm-up iterations before measurement to stabilize performance
output_contract: Scaling limit (thread count threshold) where throughput plateaus, confirmation that critical section is the bottleneck, and quantified contention signature (e.g., lock wait time, critical section occupancy percentage)

examples.input: Concurrent algorithm with centralized timestamp allocation; test with YCSB medium-contention workload
examples.output: Throughput plateaus at 20 cores; critical section occupancy exceeds 80% beyond 20 threads; scaling limit confirmed at 16–32 active threads
examples.notes: Matches expected behavior for algorithms with shared global resources

metadata.prompt: Execute a scaling test on the concurrent algorithm under evaluation. Measure throughput across increasing thread counts (e.g., 1, 4, 8, 16, 20, 32, 64 threads). Plot throughput vs. thread count. Identify the thread count threshold beyond which throughput plateaus or degrades. Confirm that the critical section (shared global state access) is the primary bottleneck by comparing lock contention metrics or profiling data. Document the scaling limit and the contention signature.
